A brand-new store section isn't a 'revision'
Politely price extra requests separately
slides.narration: Define upfront how many rounds of revision are included per listing or task - a request to build a completely new store section, rather than a tweak to existing work, isn't really a 'revision,' and it's fair to politely price that as an additional request.

slides.heading: Turning Difficult Clients Into Long-Term Ones
bullets: Most 'difficult' clients just want to feel heard
Consistent, calm communication builds trust
Know when a client truly isn't the right fit
slides.narration: Many clients who seem difficult at first just want to feel heard and kept in the loop - consistent, calm communication usually turns them into your most loyal clients over time. Occasionally, though, a client genuinely isn't the right fit, and it's okay to part ways professionally.

slides.heading: Leveling Up Your Skill Set
bullets: Learn basic paid ads (Amazon PPC, Meta Ads)
Get comfortable with simple SEO research
Study sales reports more deeply over time
slides.narration: As you grow, learning basic paid advertising like Amazon PPC or Meta Ads, getting comfortable with simple keyword and SEO research, and studying sales reports more deeply all let you charge more and take on bigger stores.

slides.heading: Deciding Between More Clients or Higher Rates
bullets: More clients means more income but more hours
Higher rates mean the same hours, more income
Most successful VAs eventually favor the second
slides.narration: At some point you'll choose between taking on more clients at your current rate, or fewer clients at a higher rate - most experienced E-commerce VAs eventually favor raising rates over endlessly adding more clients, since it protects both quality and your own time.

slides.heading: Building Toward an Agency or Team
bullets: Some VAs eventually hire their own subcontractors
Others stay solo and simply raise rates
Both paths are valid - choose what fits your goals
slides.narration: Some experienced E-commerce VAs eventually build a small team, subcontracting listing or fulfillment work to other freelancers and keeping strategy for themselves; others prefer staying solo and simply commanding premium rates. Neither path is more 'correct' - it depends on what kind of work-life you actually want.

slides.heading: Congratulations on Finishing This Training
bullets: You've covered the full E-commerce VA skillset
You have a portfolio, resume, and pricing plan
Time to start applying with confidence
slides.narration: Congratulations - you've now covered the full E-commerce VA skillset, from the tools and daily skills to portfolio-building, client acquisition, and long-term growth. You're ready to start applying and pitching with real confidence.

lessons.title: International Shipping, Customs, and Duties Basics

slides.heading: Why International Orders Get More Complex
bullets: Customs forms and duties vary a lot by destination country
Delivery times are longer and considerably less predictable
A VA often fields more 'where's my order' questions
slides.narration: International orders bring extra complexity - customs requirements and duties vary widely by destination country, delivery times run longer and less predictably, and as a result a VA usually fields more 'where's my order' questions from international buyers.

slides.heading: Customs Documentation Basics
bullets: Accurate product descriptions and declared values are required
Incorrect declarations can delay or even return a package
A consistent template helps keep this accurate order to order
slides.narration: Customs paperwork requires accurate product descriptions and honestly declared values - getting this wrong can delay a shipment or even have it returned entirely. Using a consistent template for repeat product types helps keep this accurate order after order.

slides.heading: Who Pays Duties and Taxes
bullets: DDP means the seller covers duties and taxes upfront
DDU/DAP means the customer pays duties on delivery
The store's checkout should make this clear to avoid surprises
slides.narration: DDP (Delivered Duty Paid) means the seller collects and covers duties upfront at checkout. DDU or DAP means the customer pays duties directly upon delivery instead - whichever model a client uses, the checkout page should state it clearly to avoid unhappy surprises.

slides.heading: Setting Customer Expectations for International Orders
bullets: State realistic delivery windows directly on the listing
Note that customs delays are possible and outside the seller's control
Respond patiently to anxious international buyers
slides.narration: Set realistic delivery windows right on the product listing, and note plainly that customs delays are possible and outside the seller's direct control. International buyers are often understandably anxious about their order - patient, clear communication goes a long way.

lessons.title: Working With Suppliers and Quality Control

slides.heading: Why VAs Sometimes Coordinate With Suppliers
bullets: Restocking depends on clear, timely supplier communication
Quality issues need to be tracked and reported consistently
A VA can act as the go-between for a busy store owner
slides.narration: For stores holding their own inventory, restocking depends on clear, timely communication with suppliers, and any quality issues need to be tracked and reported consistently. A VA can take on this go-between role for an owner who's stretched too thin to manage it alone.

slides.heading: Basic Supplier Communication
bullets: Confirm order quantities, costs, and lead times in writing
Follow up proactively as expected ship dates approach
Keep a simple log of every supplier order placed
slides.narration: Good supplier communication means confirming quantities, costs, and expected lead times in writing every time, following up proactively as a ship date approaches rather than waiting to be surprised, and keeping a simple running log of every order placed.

slides.heading: Spotting and Reporting Quality Issues
bullets: Watch for a spike in returns citing the same defect
Document issues clearly with photos and specific notes
Report patterns to the client promptly, not just once
slides.narration: Watch return reasons for a spike around the same defect - that's usually a sign of a real quality control issue with the supplier. Document any such issue clearly with photos and specific notes, and report the pattern to the client promptly rather than waiting to mention it once.

slides.heading: Supporting Reorders and Stock Planning
bullets: Track how fast each product sells to predict reorder timing
Flag slow-moving stock that may need a promotion instead
A simple reorder calendar prevents last-minute scrambles
slides.narration: Tracking how quickly each product sells helps predict when a reorder should go in before stock actually runs out, while flagging slow-moving items early lets the client consider a promotion instead of restocking. A simple shared reorder calendar prevents a lot of last-minute scrambling.

lessons.title: Basic Financial Reporting and COGS Awareness

slides.heading: Why Basic Financial Awareness Helps a VA
bullets: Helps you understand what 'good numbers' actually look like
Makes your reporting genuinely more useful to the client
Builds trust that you understand the business, not just tasks
slides.narration: Having even a basic grasp of a store's finances helps you understand what 'good numbers' actually look like, makes any reporting you produce genuinely more useful, and builds a client's trust that you understand their business, not just the individual tasks they hand you.

slides.heading: What COGS Means and Why It Matters
bullets: Cost of Goods Sold - what it actually costs to source a product
Revenue minus COGS gives a rough gross profit picture
Explains why a 'best-selling' item isn't always the most profitable
slides.narration: COGS, or Cost of Goods Sold, is what it actually costs a business to source or manufacture a product. Subtracting COGS from revenue gives a rough gross profit picture - and it explains why the 'best-selling' item by volume isn't always the most profitable one.

slides.heading: Simple Numbers Worth Including in Reports
bullets: Revenue and units sold by product
Estimated profit margin, if the client shares cost data
Return rate, since returns quietly eat into profit
slides.narration: Simple, useful numbers to include in a regular report are revenue and units sold by product, an estimated profit margin if the client is comfortable sharing cost data, and return rate - since a high return rate quietly erodes profit even when sales volume looks healthy.

slides.heading: Staying in Your Lane as a VA
bullets: You support reporting - you are not the client's accountant
Flag anything that looks off rather than guessing at answers
Refer real bookkeeping or tax questions to a qualified professional
slides.narration: It's important to stay in your lane here - you support reporting and pattern-spotting, but you are not the client's accountant or tax advisor. Flag anything that looks off rather than guessing, and always refer real bookkeeping or tax questions to a qualified professional.

lessons.title: Building Systems and SOPs to Save Time

slides.heading: What an SOP Is and Why It Matters
bullets: Standard Operating Procedure - a written, repeatable process
Turns a task you know well into something anyone could follow
Saves time re-explaining the same thing over and over
slides.narration: An SOP, or Standard Operating Procedure, is simply a written, repeatable process for a task you already know how to do well. Writing it down once turns it into something anyone could follow, saving you from re-explaining the same steps again and again.

slides.heading: Tasks Worth Turning Into an SOP First
bullets: Order fulfillment steps for a specific client
How to handle the most common type of customer question
The monthly reporting process, start to finish
slides.narration: Good first candidates for an SOP are a specific client's order fulfillment steps, how to handle the single most common type of customer question you get, and the full monthly reporting process from start to finish.

slides.heading: Keeping SOPs Simple and Usable
bullets: Numbered steps beat one long, dense paragraph
Screenshots make platform-specific steps much clearer
Store them somewhere easy to find and update later
slides.narration: A good SOP uses short numbered steps rather than one long paragraph, includes screenshots for anything platform-specific to make it instantly clearer, and lives somewhere easy to find and update the moment a process changes.

slides.heading: How SOPs Help You Scale
bullets: Makes it easier to bring on help as you grow
Protects a client's business if you're ever unavailable
A mark of a truly professional operation, not just a solo freelancer
slides.narration: Well-built SOPs make it far easier to eventually bring on help as you grow, protect a client if you're ever sick or unavailable, and are genuinely a mark of a professional operation - something that sets you apart from a purely one-person, everything-in-my-head freelancer.
